note: These are the ad-format comparison reels. They are not interfaces to copy - they are *proof of process*. Their value is as argument: they show what an agent that has design memory produces versus one that does not. Described here because the contrast is the artefact, and because the collection contains enough of them to establish the pattern (typography degrades first, then spacing rhythm, then colour discipline).

items.title: No skills vs MCP + Skills - the baseline comparison
items.description: Two phone mockups side by side on plain white, each with a bold black caption above it: 'No skills' on the left, 'MCP + Skills' on the right. The left device shows a pale washed-out screen with a few lines of placeholder copy and a single blue pill button sitting high on the canvas with a large ungrateful empty area beneath it. The right device is dark: a contained card with tighter, better-set copy and a deliberate amount of breathing room around it. The whole argument of the ad is carried by the *composition* rather than the copy - the left screen is under-designed (elements floating, no hierarchy, no rhythm), the right one has a clear container, a pulled-together focal point, and a coherent surface treatment. Useful as a diagnostic example of what 'generated by an agent with no design memory' looks like.
items.quality: Low information density - mostly empty space in the left panel. Read as a process artefact, not a layout reference.
items.source_note: From the MCP/skills ad-video format the user collected. Retained because the before/after claim is the thing worth studying.

items.title: Before ($10k/mo) vs After (MCP + Skills) - wallet app
items.description: A wide side-by-side of two phone screens with captions 'Before ($10k/mo)' and 'After (MCP + Skills)'. Same product in both - a crypto wallet. The 'before' screen opens onto a plain green header card with a checklist of rows, a white button, and a lot of undifferentiated vertical stacking; the 'after' screen opens onto a dark surface with a large clearly-set balance, a donut/progress ring, and transaction rows with real hierarchy. Across the strip the 'after' version consistently shows what the 'before' lacks: a single dominant number, tonal separation between sections, and consistent vertical rhythm. The $10k/mo figure frames the argument commercially rather than aesthetically.
items.quality: Good - both design states readable across the strip, so the delta can be named.
items.source_note: Ad-format comparison. Useful as evidence for what hierarchy work actually changes.

items.title: good vs better - context menu ordering and destructive-action affordance
items.description: A desktop context menu shown twice, labelled 'good' and 'better' at the top. Both panels offer the same four actions - Crop image, Move folder, Copy to clipboard, Delete image. The 'better' version makes two changes: it reorders the items so the destructive action is no longer grouped with the routine ones, and it sets 'Delete image' in red with a leading icon. A rare example in this collection of a *pure interaction-design critique* rather than an aesthetic one: nothing about the colour scheme or typography changed, only the ordering and the signalling of consequence. This is the kind of adjustment that is easy to miss and expensive to get wrong.
items.quality: Small UI region, so text is small - the structural change is legible even where individual words are not.
items.source_note: The only interaction-design (rather than visual-design) comparison in the collection.

items.title: Original vs Opus 5 vs Opus 5.5 - three generations of one screen
items.description: Three phone mockups in a row labelled 'Original', 'Opus 5' and 'Opus 5.5', all rendering the same finance app. The Original is a plain light screen with little structure. Opus 5 introduces a card carrying a large balance figure ('$6,861.76 USD') over transaction rows - the first point at which a focal hierarchy exists. Opus 5.5 refines it further, tightening the card, adjusting the type scale and settling the vertical rhythm. The value here is the middle row: it isolates the single change that does most of the work (introducing one dominant element), which is more instructive than a two-state before/after where many things change at once.
items.quality: Good. Three states rather than two makes the progression legible.
items.source_note: Model-version comparison. The three-up format is worth reusing for any progression study.

items.title: Fable 5.1 vs GPT-6 Astra - same brief, two outputs
items.description: Two phone mockups side by side, labelled 'Fable 5.1' and 'GPT-6 Astra', both answering the same app-store-screen brief. The left is a light composition with scattered blue app icons and copy about creating and discovering with tools. The right is the dark inversion of the same idea, with white icons on black and near-identical copy. The two are remarkably close in structure and differ mainly in surface and icon treatment, which is the interesting finding: given the same brief, two capable models converge on the same layout and diverge on tonality. Useful as evidence that layout conventions are much more standardised than colour choices.
items.source_note: Model-output comparison rather than a design critique. Read for the layout-convergence finding.

items.title: Same document, light theme vs dark theme
items.description: Two portrait document pages side by side on white. The left is a pale cream-green layout with small dense text blocks and a red bookmark strip running down one edge. The right is the same document rendered dark - white text on a near-black page, with a highlighted heading. A clean light/dark theme pair for a reading surface, and notably one where the dark version is a genuine restatement rather than an inversion filter: the heading treatment and the accent both change, not just the background.
items.quality: Text is dense and small, so it reads as a layout comparison rather than a copy reference.
